articles.text: Keeping with summer tradition, the City of Piedmont has hired a herd of nearly 200 goats to control the weeds in Moraga Canyon ahead of the upcoming fire season. Starting in early July, the goats were let loose onto the hillside behind the Corporation Yard in a flurry of black, white, and brown fur. The stubby-horned lawnmowers have worked across this area for the past weeks, moving soon across the road to tackle the hillside above Blair Park. Each year, the City of Piedmont competitively bids on the services of these goats in the employ of Ecosystem Concepts, a local vegetation management company. The goats are almost always in high demand for a number of reasons – they are inexpensive, better for the environment, and take care of challenging areas that would otherwise require mechanical equipment. The herd’s vegetation-eating efforts are crucial to fire prevenA pair of goats team up to take down a bush. tion, especially in the hot summer months. In the coming weeks, goats will chew their way through the overgrown brush, weeds and the lower limbs of trees behind the Corporation Yard to create a “fuel break” through which wildfires are less likely to burn. Officials hope that this effort will provide a critical buffer for homes up the hill in the event of a fire. The annual grazing usually takes around two to three weeks. The furry lawncare advocates eat for roughly eight hours in a day, with a break for rest between their morning and afternoon shifts. LETTERS - MAIN Safer plan needed for Blair Park pedestrians Editor: The city built the existing fence between the sidewalk and roadway from Red Rock Road to Monte Avenue to stop children walking to and from Coaches Field from crossing Moraga Avenue. The City Council considered the fence necessary because Caltrans standards for safe sightlines and stopping distances could not be met on Moraga Avenue at or near Red Rock Road. Recent analyses provided by independent traffic engineers show that violations of those standards remain not only between Monte Avenue and Red Rock Road but also along much of the Blair Park frontage on Moraga Avenue. Despite these violations, the draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan shows an option with 199 homes in Blair Park. Piedmonters presumably value children living in Moraga Canyon as highly as children living in central Piedmont. If so, the Specific Plan would include strategies to protect children living in Blair Park from the danger inherent in crossing Moraga Avenue to Coaches Field or to the existing fenced sidewalk they would use to walk to school and back. We have, after all, protected children walking from central Piedmont to Coaches Field even though they have little reason to cross Moraga. How, then, can we not protect children required by the Specific Plan to cross the same roadway? Sadly, the only protection offered in the Plan is to “signalize” a crossing at Red Rock Road – a location we know does not meet Caltrans safe sightlines standards. What good does it do to “signalize” an intersection that drivers will not see until it’s too late to stop? The only responsible and decent solution to this conundrum is to adopt the safer option shown in the Plan. That option would move the city corporation yard to Blair Park and locate the 199 homes around Coaches Field. The only argument publicly offered against this alternative is that the city would incur the cost of rebuilding the corporation yard. The city will, however, incur that cost whether or not new housing ever appears in Moraga Canyon. articles.text: In a time marked by escalating anti-immigrant rhetoric and policies, BBQ Without Borders will return to the Oakland Museum of California on Saturday, August 2, This popular biennial event, presented by No Immigrants No Spice (NINS), is more than just a celebration of food; it’s a powerful affirmation of the immense and often unacknowledged contributions of immigrant communities to our nation’s cultural richness and social fabric. Amidst a social context where immigrants often face disproportionate challenges, including workplace discrimination, difficulties affording basic needs, and fear related to immigration laws, BBQ Without Borders stands as a beacon of solidarity and celebration. This event is a space that uplifts the lived stories and contributions of immigrants who, despite these hurdles, are incredible drivers of growth and innovation. For instance, in 2022, immigrants were estimated to be one-quarter of America’s entrepreneurs, founding 43.8% of the Fortune 500 companies. These immigrant-founded companies employed more than 14.8 million people worldwide and generated over $7 trillion in revenue. Furthermore, immigrants contribute billions of dollars in taxes annually, with undocumented immigrants alone contributing an estimated $96.7 billion in federal, state, and local taxes in 2022. This year’s event, themed “Toward A Greener Future,” will not only highlight the economic and cultural impact of immigrants but also emphasize the valuable sustainable practices they have long contributed. From eco-friendly farming and cooking techniques rooted in ancestral wisdom, no waste whole animal and planting cooking to a deep, inherent respect for nature, immigrant communities offer crucial insights into cooking up a more sustainable tomorrow for all. This focus is particularly urgent as climate-related hazards like floods, storms, and wildfires are already a major driver of global human mobility, playing a role in 26.4 million displacements in 2023 alone. Climate change is increasingly exacerbating displacement, with the World Bank projecting that slow-onset climate disasters could drive internal displacement for as many as 216 million people by 2050 if urgent action is not taken, further underscoring the interconnectedness of climate justice and immigrant rights. Attendees will embark on an unforgettable culinary journey, savoring an incredible array of flavors from a stellar lineup of Bay Area immigrant chefs, including: • Anthony Salguero of Popoca: Bringing Salvadoran-inspired delights to the forefront. • The team at Café Colucci: Serving up their renowned Ethiopian cuisine. • Maria Marquez of Tacos Mama Cuca: Offering delicious traditional and modern Mexican flavors from Sonora. • Desserts from Third Culture Bakery: A sweet Indonesian and Taiwanese inspired finish to an exceptional meal. Beyond the mouth-watering food and vibrant performances, BBQ Without Borders is a critical fundraiser for the East Bay immigrant community. Their ambitious goal this year is to raise $50,000 in mutual aid. “In a time when the narratives around immigration are often distorted, BBQ Without Borders offers a tangible space with a delicious counter-narrative,” said Piedmont resident Dr. Vibha Gupta, founder of No Immigrants No Spice. “We believe that by coming together over food, we can bridge divides, celebrate the cultural richness immigrants bring, and directly support those who are building our communities from the ground up.” BBQ Without Borders will be held on Saturday, August 2 from 3:00 - 7:00 p.m. at Oakland Museum of California. Tickets are now available at https:// events.humanitix.com/bbq-without-borders-2025/tickets, and various ticket tiers are available. Join for an afternoon that nourishes both body and soul, where every bite supports a more inclusive and equitable future. Organizers encourage people to come hungry, leave inspired, and help celebrate the invaluable tapestry that immigrants weave into the fabric of their communities. No Immigrants No Spice (NINS) is a non-profit organization that uses food as a way to highlight the positive impact immigrants have on culture and society. Through events and initiatives like BBQ Without Borders, NINS aims to foster understanding, celebrate diversity, and provide critical support to immigrant communities, including the distribution of micro-grants. Learn more at https://noimmigrantsnospice.org/.

articles.text: The city of Piedmont is asking community members to share feedback on the city’s Draft Local Hazard Mitigation Plan—a roadmap outlining what Piedmont could do now to reduce or avoid potential damage from natural hazards like earthquakes, wildfires and severe weather—online, by email or mail, or at one of two upcoming meetings. The Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP): • Identifies the natural hazards that pose the greatest risk to Piedmont • Describes how each hazard would likely impact Piedmont if it occurred • Identifies and prioritizes actions the city and community could take now to prevent or reduce those impacts The draft LHMP is the result of nine months of research, discussion and public engagement. Gathering community input is the final step before the city finalizes the document and submits it to Cal OES for approval. Community members may submit comments online or by email to lhmp@piedmont.ca.gov. A presentation on the draft LHMP was held at the Public Safety Committee meeting on Thursday, July 24, and a meeting of the Hazard Mitigation Planning Committee took place on Friday, July 25. Details about upcoming meetings are available at piedmont. ca.gov/LHMP. Priority actions to reduce risk The draft LHMP identifies 21 actions that could help reduce risk in Piedmont, including: • Strengthening IT infrastructure through redundancy and backup systems • Retrofitting or replacing critical facilities to meet modern seismic safety codes • Conducting annual fire fuel mitigation on city property • Strengthening building and fire codes to require wildfire-resistant construction and more stringent vegetation management standards Including an action in the LHMP does not guarantee implementation. Rather, it helps position the city to apply for state and federal mitigation grants that could support the proposed project. Learn more about the Local Hazard Mitigation Plan update process and read the draft plan at piedmont.ca.gov/LHMP. Get notified directly of upcoming meetings, events, and engagement opportunities by subscribing to email updates at piedmont. ca.gov/LHMPnews. With questions, comments, or requests to get more involved, email LHMP@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: “I was so excited my voice wouldn’t come out of my mouth!! I was trying to signal to everyone - it’s there! It’s there! And once we saw it everyone was just jumping!” What exactly sparked this level of excitement from Dr. Alejandra Hernandez, coral reef scientist at the California Academy of Sciences? A huge, deep-dwelling hammerhead shark, spotted on her very first submarine descent! Dr. Hernandez’s work to understand marine ecosystems spans both shallow and deep coral reefs. Using innovative technology including robotics, 3D photography, and genetic sequencing, the team gathers data on the flora and fauna found in these ocean ecosystems, monitoring where corals grow and their health, near the surface and at deeper depths. Academy chair of aquatic biology Dr. Pim Bongaertz explains that sometimes the same species of coral grows near the surface and in the depths. The conditions are so different - how does coral do that? Understanding the answer may enable solutions that increase coral reef resiliency around the world. In search of answers to this and other pressing questions facing marine ecosystems, Drs. Bongaertz and Hernandez have “blue careers,” working to advance marine conservation. Dr. Bongaertz is quick to point out that his lab will not single-handedly solve the critical problems facing coral reefs, rather they are providing an important piece of the puzzle being worked on by scientists all over the globe. Collaboration is a critical ingredient for success, spanning scientists, communities, policy makers, financers, educators and more. All of these collaborators have exciting blue careers too, supporting an entire “blue economy.” To ensure healthy marine life, thriving coastal communities, and a robust “blue economy,” it’s crucial to engage young people. School programs at the California Academy of Sciences offer ocean related museum field trips to K-5 students, opportunities to connect with scientists working in “blue careers,” and more. Through engaging activities and stories students realize science is for everyone and needs everyone! Students also practice the transformative skill of collaboration. A third grader explains: “Collaboration for scientists is important because it can help them finish a task and help others. They can share knowledge with each other. It is important, too, because if they get into a bad situation, they can help each other get out of it.” Interested in seeing what it’s like to descend into the deep in a submarine like Dr. Hernandez, or learn about some of the technology illuminating the secrets of the deep? Unseen Oceans, on view at the California Academy of Sciences through September 7, gives visitors of all ages the opportunity to discover the dazzling creatures and features of the deep ocean, and to explore the exciting, collaborative “blue careers” that await the next generation of scientists as they puzzle out a thriving future for these precious ecosystems. articles.text: questions. All three Piedmont elementary schools were named California Distinguished Schools in 2023, under the same two criteria. That year, 22 elementary schools in Alameda County were recognized, compared to just 13 in 2025. The significant drop has led some to wonder if there was an informal quota by region, or whether the state prioritized schools demonstrating progress in underserved populations. The Piedmont Post reached out to Thurmond’s office for clarification but did not receive a response by press time. The Distinguished Schools program alternates annually between elementary and secondary school recipients. In 2024, middle and high schools were eligible. Piedmont Middle School received the honor in both 2019 and 2021. No awards were given in 2022 due to the pandemic. Selection for the program is based on metrics from the California School Dashboard, the state’s multi-indicator accountability system. “The California Department of Education (CDE) uses multiple measures to identify eligible schools based on their performance on the state indicators as specified on the California School Dashboard,” Thurmond’s press release stated.

All three Piedmont elementary schools were named California Distinguished Schools in 2023, under the same two criteria. That year, 22 elementary schools in Alameda County were recognized, compared to just 13 in 2025. articles.text: The opening of a new memorial mediation garden at Piedmont Community Church was celebrated on church grounds during a dedication ceremony on Saturday, July 12. The garden, which includes a labyrinth and fountain, is dedicated to church member Judy Wright’s husband, Bob, who died in JanChurch member Sonja ten Grotenhuis brought the garden to life as a Girl Scout Gold Award Project within Girl Scout Troop 33426. Church members Suzie Skugstad, Paul Schroeder and a host of volunteers dedicated time to create the garden and donations from church members and friends paid for construction. Around 30 people attended the dedication ceremony which included speeches, the singing of Amazing Grace and a prayer over the garden by Senior Pastor Don Ashburn to conclude the dedication. Ashburn also spoke to those gathered about the significance of the labyrinth portion of the garden. The sacred space is open to the community for quiet meditation and reflection. Walkers of the labyrinth are encouraged to stop at the rock fountain in the center to say a prayer and give their burdens to God. As ten Grotenhuis’ Gold Award project, the memorial garden signified the completion of the most honored achievement a Girl Scout can earn, comparable to an Eagle project. All Gold Award projects require more than 80 hours of work but Scouts spend years preparing and making decisions on what kind of project to bring to life. articles.text: Piedmont City Council voted at their meeting on Monday, July 7, to approve a contract for street paving to contractor McGuire and Hester for $1,370,000, with an overall construction budget of $1.5 million. This project will remove and replace asphalt on 10 residential streets this summer, as well as restriping markings on 32 additional roadways. The residential repaving project calls for as much as 2,000 tons of hot mix asphalt in its repairs. It is also expected to have 4,200 square feet of roadway dig-outs, and repair 650 feet of gutter. Work locations are concentrated primarily in the Dracena Park area, between Grand and Highland Avenues. According to the Public Works Department the selection of streets was based upon streets with the most vehicle miles on them. This work is separate from the ongoing Grand Avenue Repavement Project, which is adding pedestrian safety features to the section of Grand Avenue in Piedmont. “We are removing and replacing existing asphalt,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. A work schedule for the project is expected in August. Public Works plans to notify residents of affected streets once the schedule is available, through flyers and other communication methods. For streets near schools, the City plans to coordinate with schools to minimize potential disruptions. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Toledo Blade Tadej Pogačar wins his fourth Tour de France title in six years. Tadej Pogačar continues to prove he’s a once in a generation type of athlete, winning this year’s Tour de France, marking his fourth title in six years. He is now equal on wins with Chris Froome, one behind France’s Jacques Anquetilm and Bernard Hinault, and two back of Belgian legend Eddy Merckx, and Miguel Induráin of Spain. Pogačar won the General Classification’ Yellow Jersey with a 4 minute, 24 second lead over Danish rival Jonas Vingegaard. It now marks the second consecutive year for Vingegaard to trail Pogačar after the Dane beat the Slovenian in 2022 and 2023. He captured four stage wins to help establish a four-minute lead with eight stages remaining. Also winning the Polka Dot Jersey for being the top Mountain Classification rider, Pogačar excelled on the hilly and mountain courses. He won Stage 4’s 108.2 mile hilly course and Stage 7’s 122 mile hilly course before making his push on the Stage 12-13 mountain ride. Pogačar won Stage 12’s 112.2 mile ride through the Pyrenees mountains with a sturdy 2 minutes, 10 second lead on Vingegaard in second. The Slovenian then won Stage 13’s 6.8 mile time trial in the Pyrenees with a 36 second advantage over Vingegaard, creating a 4 minute and 7 second lead in the process. articles.text: Richey recounts attaining No. 1 in the U.S. and subsequent work in mental-health awareness Photo courtesy of Cliff Richey A newspaper clipping of Cliff Richey’s monumental sudden-death victory over Stan Smith at the Berkeley Tennis Club’s Pacific Coast Championship in 1970. [Reprinted from October 2020] Back in the late 60s and early 70s, some of the best tennis players in the world would’ve been gathering in the shadows of the Claremont Hotel at the Berkeley Tennis Club around the start of October. The Pacific Coast Championship ran from 1889 to 2013, it was the second oldest ongoing tennis tourney in the United States and is predated only by the U.S. Open. With the start of tennis’ Open Era beginning in 1968, the final three years of the Pacific Coast Championships’ run in Berkeley from ’68 to 1971 meant the best players in the world were meeting close by. Many inf luential matches were taking place for the endof-year rankings, given an October championship meant it was among the final tournaments to determine the leaderboard. Back in 1970, that meant Cliff Richey squaring off with former Wimbledon and US Open champion Stan Smith for the No. 1 ranking in the United States in the semifinals of the Pacific Coast Championship in one of the most breathtaking matches ever played. Their match ran over four hours long and was perhaps the only time a No. 1 ranking came down to a sudden-death point. The score was 7-6, 6-7, 6-3, 6-4, and 4-4 in the final set with the next point the end-all, win-all. Richey hit a forehand volley for the winner. “Almost any way you cut it, the Pacific Coast Championship in Berkeley was the last event of the year for international players… That year going into the tournament, I knew I was in the running for the No. 1 ranking in the United States,” explained Richey from his home in San Angelo, Texas now 73-years old, describing that the U.S. ranking system. “That match was such an unusual finish; it went literally down to the last ball. I had a second serve in my hand at four points all, six-all in the fifth set after playing for four hours, it was ridiculous!” added Richey about the match. Richey’s victory over Smith also meant that he was on pace to win tennis’ world point system under the International Tennis Federation’s Grand Prix circuit, which was famously the predecessor of the current ATP Tour. “In addition, that match was also important because that was the first year the International Tennis Federation Grand Prix of tennis, which was a point system and started at the French Open and finished in Europe. I knew at the Berkeley event that I was doing well in the Grand Prix. “I went to Europe after beating Stan and beat Ken Rosewall in the semifinals London event, and I knew I had to win two matches in Stockholm the next week. The other player right on my butt was Arthur Ashe, but he had to win Stockholm… So the match against Stan also enabled me to win the Grand Prix,” explained Richey. Richey lost to Hall of Famer Arthur Ashe in the 1970 Pacific Coast Championship finals, but his No. 1 ranking was already solidified the previous round. “All the players, officials, or anybody who was close to the game knew that my match with Stan Smith in the semifinals would be for the No. 1 ranking regardless of what happened in the finals,” he said. Following his tennis career, Richey became an activist for mental health awareness after dealing with bouts of clinical depression. articles.text: Husband and wife textile artists Agus Ismoyo and Nia Fliam host a batik workshop at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco this Sunday, August 3. Batik fabricmaking, originating from Indonesia and Java, has been celebrated for centuries. It still remains a large part of the culture of Indonesia and is widely used in celebrations and rituals, including marriage ceremonies and religious observations. The fabric is made using a wax and resist dyeing technique and has been mastered by artists and families for over 2000 years. Ismoyo and Fliam have been producing batik textiles in their Yogyakarta, Indonesia studio since 1985. They use the traditions of Ismoyo’s ancestors, batik makers in the court city of Solo in Java, and other historical batiks as contemporary art. Their studio produces high-end batik fabrics and paintings along with a range of wearable art and interior decor. The artists will offer a hands-on workshop at 1 p.m. inviting guests to create their own batik patterns. The workshop is suitable for families with children of all ages. The workshop will be followed by storytelling. The workshop is part of the museum’s free “First Sundays,” an event that invites visitors to enjoy cultural celebrations, hands-on workshops, dance and music performances, food popups and tastings, group tours, and other community events, as well as the museum’s world-renowned collection and special exhibitions. For more information, visit https://calendar.asianart.org/ event/batik-workshop-with-agusismoyo-and-nia-fliam/.

articles.text: Docent tours held Tues through Sun Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art, the first exhibition to highlight Thiebaud’s extensive reinterpretations of works by his artistic heroes, leaves the Legion of Honor on August 17. Docent tours are held Tuesday through Sunday through Friday, August 15. The exhibition includes 65 pieces by Thiebaud, representing his wide-ranging reinterpretations of old and new European and American artworks spanning from 1957 to 2020. Thiebaud was an American painter known for his colorful works depicting commonplace objects like pies, pastries, and hot dogs, most often associated with the Pop art movement because of his interest in objects of mass culture. Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art is the first exhibition to spotlight his extensive involvement with art history throughout his six-decade-long career until his death in 2021. The exhibition is a facet of the “Legion of Honor 100,” a yearlong centennial celebration of San Francisco’s fine arts museums and its collections. “As a self-identified ‘thief,’ who mined the work of his predecessors and contemporaries, Wayne Thiebaud’s practice was deeply rooted in his study of art history, but this aspect of his work has never been explored,” said Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Over the course of the next year, as we reflect upon the Legion of Honor’s legacy as a center of art historical research and inspiration, Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art couldn’t be more timely.” Exhibition curator Timothy Anglin Burgard said Thiebaud’s engagement with art history at large “revealed his belief that the world of art transcended limiting definitions of time and place, as well as progress.” “Viewed from this perspective, the entire global history of art, encompassing every movement and style, was as accessible, relevant, and inspiring to Thiebaud as contemporary art,” he said. Special exhibition tickets are required to join docent-led tours. Tours are held Tuesdays through Sundays, at 11:30 a.m. and 1:30 p.m. Docents will be available in galleries to answer questions between August 2 and August 15. Visit https://www.famsf.org to learn more and to plan your visit. Photo courtesy of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco Guests view Wayne Thiebaud: Art Comes from Art display at Legion of Honor

articles.text: Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon in The Trip to Spain When the first of these road trip movies appeared in 2010 and Steve Coogan and Bob Brydon took a culinary tour of England, I missed it. That film was followed in 2014 by visits to similar Michelin restaurants and five star hotels as they wandered through Italy. That led to The Trip to Spain, their third adventure-lite excursion through the rolling, bucolic hills of Spain, once again taking a week to stop at historic stone hotels, each at least several hundred years old, as well as renowned restaurants that serve cuisine on white oval plates that prove to be works of art. But the essence of these trips – adapted from a BBC series – is the conversation that Coogan and Brydon engage in as they sit across from one another, their elbows leaning on white table clothes while sipping robust local wines. So therein is the full reveal. There is no plot per se. Nada. Okay, there is a fragile, oblique theme in The Trip to Spain, one hidden in all their smart banter and endless impressions of the likes of Michael Caine or Sean Connery, enhanced with spot on Mick Jagger mimicry. That theme? It’s about confronting the reality that they have arrived at that point in life just beyond middle age. And as much as that seems to matter to them, the improvisational dialogue never takes a deep dive into this existential question, one that is instead studiously ignored in favor of verbal play and clever ripostes. There are private moments when the two pause and make contact with family back home and in a way those conversations are more engaging than the riffs that take place over dinner. I know that sounds heretical, for it is these back and forth musings and comedic retorts that take stage center and engage what I can only assume is an acquired taste. I do acknowledge that British humor can be dry as day-old toast. Sara Couden, contralto Zachary Gordin, piano

By Chris Honoré The debut Prime streaming series Ballard is based on the best-selling novels written by the prolific Michael Connelly. It is not only exceptional in plotting and overall production but in characterization. It introduces Connelly’s first lead female character, detective Renée Ballard. It follows the compelling Prime series The Lincoln Lawyer and Bosch/Bosch Legacy, each based on novels by Connelly. Ballard is set in Los Angeles where, for reasons explored in some detail in the series, Ballard is given the lead in LAPD’s Cold Case division. She and a crew of volunteers and three reserve officers are given the task of taking deep dives into murders committed years ago and never solved. Though underfunded, and located in an expansive basement which is filled with shelved boxes of dormant cases. Ballard and team bring to each unsolved a renewed determination, state-ofthe-art technology (e.g. DNA/Ballistics), and what is referred to as the “murder book,” meaning the investigation’s detailed chronology and summary assembled by the original assigned detective. Ballard also finds herself coping with the seemingly inherent sexism of the LAPD. It soon See Ballard on page 31 Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon in The Trip to Spain By Chris Honoré When the first of these road trip movies appeared in 2010 and Steve Coogan and Bob Brydon took a culinary tour of England, I missed it. That film was followed in 2014 by visits to similar Michelin restaurants and five star hotels as they wandered through Italy. That led to The Trip to Spain, their third adventure-lite excursion through the rolling, bucolic hills of Spain, once again taking a week to stop at historic stone hotels, each at least several hundred years old, as well as renowned restaurants that serve cuisine on white oval plates that prove to be works of art. But the essence of these trips – adapted from a BBC series – is the conversation that Coogan and Brydon engage in as they sit across from one another, their elbows leaning on white table clothes while sipping robust local wines. So therein is the full reveal. There is no plot per se. Nada. Okay, there is a fragile, oblique theme in The Trip to Spain, one hidden in all their smart banter and endless impressions of the likes of Michael Caine or Sean Connery, enhanced with spot on Mick Jagger mimicry. That theme? It’s about confronting the reality that they have arrived at that point in life just beyond middle age. And as much as that seems to matter to them, the improvisational dialogue never takes a deep dive into this existential question, one that is instead studiously ignored in favor of verbal play and clever ripostes. There are private moments when the two pause and make contact with family back home and in a way those conversations are more engaging than the riffs that take place over dinner. I know that sounds heretical, for it is these back and forth musings and comedic retorts that take stage center and engage what I can only assume is an acquired taste. I do acknowledge that British humor can be dry as day-old toast. The time is the early 1900s and the world is on the cusp of WWI. Geppetto has been hired to carve a massive crucifix for the local church. Of course Carlo is at his side, helping, his favorite pine cone always nearby. While working, Carlo hears the sounds of planes overhead and tells his father who grows concerned. He tells Carlo that they must leave the church and hurry home. Just as they are leaving, Carlo remembers he has forgotten his pine cone and runs back into the church to find it. Meanwhile one of the planes has dropped a bomb that hits the church, killing Carlo who is still inside. Geppetto, stunned and knocked off his feet by the blast, finds the body of Carlo lying near a pew. Holding his son in his arms, he is inconsolable, his grief and sense of loss are beyond comprehension. Tearfully, he buries Carlo along with the pine cone, and so years pass. Geppetto’s sadness only increases and he takes to drink, trying to lose himself in the bottle. Italy, now controlled by Il Dulce, has become a fascist state while supporting Germany as it prepares for WWII. And then, unexpectedly, in a grief-stricken drunken rage, Geppetto goes to Carlo’s grave site and with an ax chops down the pine tree that has grown by Carlo’s tombstone. His legs are long and spindly, his nose too long, his body round and wooden. And, of course, there is no star for Geppetto to wish upon. Cricket (Ewan McGregor), the story’s narrator, watches, life is bestowed on the wooden marionette. The villagers think of the wooden youngster as a demon. It’s structured by soft tannins and juicy acidity and a smooth satisfying finish. How? By giving the gift of life insurance. Here are just a few ways you can use this proven method to contribute money to your favorite causes: • Donate an existing policy — If you already have a policy and no longer need the death benefit, you can gift the policy to your desired charity, which may give you some tax benefits. The charity will receive the full benefit amount when you die. • List the charity as a beneficiary — As the owner, you remain in control of your policy and can leave money to as many beneficiaries as you like: children, grandchildren— even multiple charities. Or, you can name a single charity the sole beneficiary, and it will receive the entire amount. • Purchase a separate policy — There are times when it makes sense to have separate policies: one for loved ones and one for charitable gifts. articles.text: Eventually, we all reach a point where it’s time to make a change and downsize—whether that means moving into a smaller home or condo, relocating to be closer to children/grandchildren, or transitioning to an independent living community that offers connection and a sense of belonging. You’ll likely have many questions about the downsizing process. Over the past year, I’ve covered a variety of topics to help guide you through this transition and am always happy to answer any questions when the time comes for you to make your move. Here’s one important aspect of selling a home to consider: understanding the buyer mindset in our area. Even the nicer homes can take a bit longer to sell these days. Here are a few reasons we counseled our clients to reduce the price; and within an hour, activity picked up and we had multiple showings, two offers and went into contract shortly thereafter. Here’s Why: You might imagine a buyer would just make a lower offer on a home. In our area, things just don’t seem to change. While in other parts of the country buyers do make lower offers, we have always been unique. We also led the way providing disclosures ahead of time in order to obtain non contingent offers. It irritated our Contra Costa and San Francisco agents until they started following suit. Why a price reduction can be a powerful strategy. • Most Buyers Do Not Want to “Offend” the Seller. Many buyers (and even their agents) hesitate to write low offers. They fear being rejected or seen as disrespectful. Instead of writing a lower offer, they often just move on to homes priced within their perceived value range. Believe me, agents do encourage agents/ buyers to come to the table. • The Market Has Spoken. You’ve had showings but no offers, which likely means buyers see better value elsewhere. A price adjustment isn’t a failure; it’s a strategic move to reposition your home to meet the market where it is today, not where it was a month ago. • Perception Is Everything. A listing that lingers over 30 days can develop a stigma— buyers may assume something’s “wrong” even if there isn’t. A fresh price can create urgency and renew interest, especially among those who may have seen the listing before. • Our Goal Is To Spark Action, Not Wait. Ultimately, the goal is to get you the highest possible price in today’s market. Strategic pricing is what drives competition—when buyers see value, they act quickly. Sometimes, a small price correction can lead to multiple offers or a faster sale than continuing to wait at a stagnant price. And so it is! A quick note to buyers: Don’t wait. Make the offer before you risk losing the home or facing competition. You might have had the chance to negotiate—before it was too late. It seems like I’m always having to click in several places when I want to save my work, when I want to cut something or copy and paste, etc. I spent so much time with this busy work that I am not spending enough time writing. Is there some way for me to speed up and smooth out my workflow? –Arthur, Piedmont Dear Arthur: When we used pen and paper, all we had to worry about was not losing the notebook we were writing in. But with computers, there are many more points of failure. And there are also many more tasks to protect what we’re doing, to edit our work, and to save our work. I think with what you describe, you would really benefit from learning a few keyboard shortcuts. Keyboard shortcuts are keyboard combinations that do the same tasks as you do when clicking around the computer. For example, when you’re writing a document in Microsoft Word, to save your work, you must go to the top of your screen, click on File, then click on Save. A shortcut using your computer keyboard would be to hold the Command button down with your thumb, and press the letter S. It doesn’t sound like it would save much time, but when you’re saving your work every few paragraphs, it is faster. The same kind of process goes for Copy and Paste. If you want to copy a selection in your document, you can highlight it with your cursor, go up to the word Edit choose Copy then click your curser in the document where you want to paste this text, and then back up to Edit and Paste. articles.text: Havens’ Avenue of Palms was for sale in 1922. They hired Houghton Sawyer, Albert Farr and Engineer Robert E. Carney to design a model city center. Continuing Farr’s Spanish Mission design at City Hall, their Master Plan called for an elaborate Exedra at the entrance to Piedmont Park, a grand threestory City Hall, additions to the current City Hall, a library, museum and municipal garages. They planned to re-route the streetcar line into a tunnel where passengers could enter and exit streetcars at an elegant plaza with a fountain at the park level. Passengers would not have to cross the streetcar tracks. The Master Plan was to be completed in phases, with each building to be approved by voters before construction. The grand three-story City Hall was scaled down to the present onestory Community Hall. Voters approved the first phase in 1924 which included funds to build the Exedra and the Community Hall. Later units of the Master Plan were never realized. School construction took precedence. The Junior High School and Wildwood School were built in 1923. Later bond issues failed to pass, and the Depression ended all thoughts of grand new construction. Piedmont’s new Community Hall and Exedra opened on April 3, 1925. Civic leaders and residents entered the newly landscaped Piedmont Park through the Exedra, which reporters compared to the “Arch of Triumph.” Guests admired Howard Gilkey’s new landscape design, with its rose garden behind the Exedra, extensive lawns and flowering shrubs along the path to the hall. The Community Hall was dedicated as a meeting place and social hall for all Piedmont residents. The lower level of the hall became the new armory for Piedmont’s Battery D of the 143rd Field Artillery. Piedmont Park had been saved The original Piedmont High School designed by William Weeks in 1921. from development. Only two small parts of the original park were sold to real estate developers. The land that became Guilford Road was sold as “Guilford Place” in 1921, and the land that became Palm Drive was sold as the Lower Piedmont Park Tract in 1922. Today, a few palm trees survive on Palm Drive from Havens’ “Avenue of Palms.” The new Community Hall and Exedra in 1925. articles.text: Frank C. Havens opened Piedmont Park in 1898 with a new Clubhouse, the mineral springs, a rustic teahouse, and the beauty of the ravine, waterfalls and meandering paths through bucolic Bushy Dell Canyon. Havens added “The Maze” (1904), an “Avenue of Palms” to the Maze from Grand Avenue, a Japanese Tea House (1907) and the Piedmont Art Gallery (1907). He added a bandstand for Sunday concerts, rustic park benches the upper park and exotic plants including Queen palm trees, Canary Island date palms, cordyline and banana trees, orchids and roses. Piedmont Park thrived until 1916. They hired Houghton Sawyer, Albert Farr and Engineer Robert E. Carney to design a model city center. Continuing Farr’s Spanish Mission design at City Hall, their Master Plan called for an elaborate Exedra at the entrance to Piedmont Park, a grand threestory City Hall, additions to the current City Hall, a library, museum and municipal garages. They planned to re-route the streetcar line into a tunnel where passengers could enter and exit streetcars at an elegant plaza with a fountain at the park level.
